basis: two ways, one of life and one of death
note: The commentary contrasts the share chosen in present life with the better Hereafter and the fire awaiting the worst; the Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death, framing the moral choice as a path with opposed outcomes.

basis: ban on divination and related practices
note: The Didache tells its reader not to become a diviner or seek such practices. Though it does not name arrows, it provides an early Christian prohibition of the divinatory aim that the commentary identifies in lot-arrows.

basis: Spirit apportions gifts individually as it wills
note: The one Spirit distributes gifts to each person individually as it wills. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's measured portion given by a determining giver rather than won in a game.

basis: fire tests each builder's work
note: The commentary moves from craft preparation and fire used to straighten a staff to the condemned entering fire; Paul says the Day reveals each person's building work and fire tests it, shifting fire from the final punishment to an assay of workmanship.

basis: fire tests each person's work
note: The day reveals each person's work because it is disclosed in fire, which tests its quality. This gives a distinct Christian use of fire as testing crafted work, beside the commentary's staff-shaping fire and punitive fire.

basis: builder saved through the fire
note: The commentary's condemned person enters the great fire, while its craft scene uses fire to correct a stick; Paul says a builder's work may burn while the builder himself is saved, even as through fire, distinguishing tested work from final destruction.

basis: God gives growth after planting and watering
note: The commentary glosses the Rab family as bringing something through stages toward completion; Paul distinguishes planting and watering from God's giving the growth, a compact image of development that culminates through divine action.

basis: hidden darkness and heart-intentions disclosed at judgment
note: The Lord brings to light what is hidden in darkness and discloses the purposes of hearts. It gives a specific New Testament development of concealed knowledge becoming morally consequential.

basis: what the Lord assigned and the path each person walks
note: Each person is to walk as the Lord assigned and as God called. The verse closely unites an apportioned share with a directed way of life.

basis: the measure and field God apportioned
note: Paul refuses to boast beyond the measure of the field God apportioned to him. The passage uses an assigned measure as a real limit and vocation, preserving both senses in the commentary's قدر.

basis: scripture is profitable for instruction
note: The commentary presents the reminder conditionally in terms of benefit; Timothy says scripture is useful for teaching, correction, and training, making the ethical usefulness of instruction explicit in a Christian context.

basis: Scripture profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training
note: Scripture is called profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. It gives a direct Christian account of how a reminder can be beneficial rather than merely repeated.

basis: person of God made complete and equipped
note: The stated result of useful instruction is that God's person becomes complete and equipped for every good work. This translates the commentary's prepared, finished artisan object into moral and communal formation.

basis: lot selects Matthias after prayer
note: The commentary identifies the forbidden game as arrow-drawn allocation of shares; Acts describes the gathered disciples praying and casting lots to select Matthias, a communal appointment rather than a distribution game.

basis: Matthias selected when the lot falls to him
note: After prayer, the apostles cast lots and Matthias receives the lot for the apostolic vacancy. It is a concrete Christian counterpart for lot as discerned communal selection rather than camel-game distribution.

basis: appointed times and territorial boundaries
note: Paul says the creator determined the allotted periods and boundaries of the nations. The text extends measured creation into fixed historical limits, the same measure-and-end dimension developed from قدّر.

basis: share in the inheritance of the saints in light
note: The Father qualifies believers for a share in the inheritance of the saints in light. It supplies the positive eschatological share that the commentary contrasts with having no share in the hereafter.

basis: inheritance received according to a prior divine purpose
note: The community receives an inheritance after being predestined according to God's purpose. It joins an allotted share to prior determination, a close counterpart to the commentary's measured portion.

basis: God's workmanship, created and prepared for a walk
note: Believers are God's workmanship, created for works God prepared beforehand so that they would walk in them. The verse makes creation a crafted making with a prepared direction of travel.

basis: maturity and the measure of full stature
note: The community is brought to a mature person and the measure of Christ's full stature. It offers a Christian development of the commentary's phase-by-phase movement to a completed limit.

basis: better and abiding possession
note: The commentary contrasts preference for present life with the better, more lasting Hereafter; Hebrews says believers accept loss of possessions because they know they have a better and abiding possession, spelling out that temporal-versus-enduring choice.

basis: discipline for good and a share in holiness
note: God's discipline is for the hearers' good so that they may share in holiness. The verse joins staged parental formation, benefit, and received share, three elements the commentary develops separately.

basis: do not refuse the one who speaks
note: The readers are warned not to refuse the one who speaks from heaven. It is a direct continuation of the response contrast in 87:9-11: warning becomes deadly when its speaker is avoided.

basis: hearing God's voice rather than hardening the heart
note: The exhortation says that when God's voice is heard, hearers must not harden their hearts. It is a close response-pattern counterpart to the wretched person who keeps away from the reminder.

basis: nothing hidden from God's sight
note: The commentary's 87:7 says God knows what is aloud and what is hidden; Hebrews says no creature is hidden from God's sight and all is exposed before him, a direct counterpart to the hidden side of that claim.

basis: no creature hidden before God
note: No creature is hidden from God's sight; all are exposed before the one to whom account is given. This follows the same speaker, hiddenness, and accountability structure as 87:7.

basis: not a forgetful hearer, but a doer blessed in action
note: James contrasts a forgetful hearer with one who persists in the liberating law and is blessed in doing. It gives the commentary's beneficial reminder a practical outcome rather than mere recollection.

basis: Aramaic rabbi, teacher, and Arabic rabb
note: The source commentary labels the ayah's رَبّ with root r-b-b and glosses a family of nurturing and completing senses; John's Greek text preserves the Aramaic address Rabbi and explains it as Teacher, a related Semitic authority term with a narrower use here.

basis: the shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
note: The shepherd brings out his own sheep, goes before them, and they follow. This gives a close living analogue to the commentary's leading staff, named for preceding the one it guides.

basis: Spirit of truth guides into all truth
note: The Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth. It supplies a distinctly Christian form of the commentary's guidance motif, where leading reaches truthful understanding rather than a physical target.

basis: lot for the un-torn tunic
note: The commentary describes a camel cut into pieces and shares assigned by arrows; John says the soldiers cast lots for Jesus' seamless tunic rather than tear it, an adjacent but distinct use of lots to allocate a possession.

basis: priestly service assigned by lot
note: Zechariah receives the sanctuary task by lot under priestly custom. This is a Christian-scriptural instance of a regulated sacred lot, to be read beside the commentary's sharply negative treatment of divinatory or gambling arrows.

basis: chosen portion that remains
note: The commentary reads 87:16–17 as preferring one share over another and calls the Hereafter better and more enduring; Jesus says Mary chose the good portion that will not be taken away, a close image of a selected, lasting share.

basis: whispered words proclaimed from rooftops
note: The commentary says God knows what is aloud and what is hidden; Jesus says what was spoken in the dark and whispered in inner rooms will be heard and proclaimed publicly, a specific speech-level counterpart that turns secrecy into disclosure.

basis: worldly good reversed after death
note: The commentary contrasts preference for present life with the better lasting Hereafter; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in his life while Lazarus received bad, but their conditions are reversed after death, a narrative counterpart to the choice's final share.

basis: Isaiah's crooked roads made straight in John the Baptist's preparation
note: Luke places the leveling of valleys, straightening of crooked places, and smoothing of rough ways in the preparation for the Lord's coming. It is a specifically Christian reading of the road-making image that the commentary hears in سوّى and هدى.

basis: fresh wineskins preserve what they contain
note: New wine must be put into fresh wineskins so that both vessel and wine are preserved. Its point depends on the condition and fitness of worked leather containers, an apt counterpart to the commentary's detailed water-skin craftsmanship.

basis: gaining the world at the cost of life
note: The commentary says people prefer present life although the Hereafter is better and more enduring; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life, making the cost of that preference explicit.

basis: Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire applied to Gehenna
note: Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire in teaching about Gehenna. This Christian reuse gives the Isaiah image an explicitly punitive afterlife setting beside the commentary's great fire.

basis: easy yoke and light burden
note: Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light. This is a close Christian use of ease as the character of a divinely given way, beside 87:8's promise of being eased toward ease.

basis: condemned sent to eternal fire
note: The commentary's 87:11–12 moves from avoiding the reminder to entering the great fire; Matthew's judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire, a direct eschatological fire counterpart with its own judgment setting.

basis: eternal fire prepared for the cursed
note: The cursed are told to depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. This is a distinct Christian judgment scene for the great fire, with preparation language that also recalls the commentary's crafted readiness.

basis: easy road leads to destruction
note: The commentary says God makes the way easy for the addressed messenger and then describes avoidance of the reminder and the great fire; Matthew calls the broad, easy way destruction-bound. The link is limited because the easy way has a different referent, but the contrast makes ease point toward opposite outcomes.

basis: hard way leads to life
note: The commentary associates divine facilitation with ease and sets successful guidance against the fire; Matthew says the narrow, hard way leads to life, an explicit reversal of the easy/destructive route in the neighboring verse, though the addressees and settings differ.

basis: the measure used returns to the measurer
note: The measure used in judgment is measured back to the judge. It turns the commentary's measuring vocabulary into an ethical rule of reciprocal assessment.

basis: begun work brought to completion
note: The one who began a good work will bring it to completion. Its beginning-to-finish divine workmanship closely parallels the commentary's account of ربّ as completing what is gradually made.

basis: measuring reed or rod for temple, altar, and worshipers
note: John is given a reed like a rod and commanded to measure the temple, altar, and worshipers. The passage preserves the joined material images of a staff-like implement and exact measurement.

basis: golden measuring rod for city, gates, and wall
note: The angel holds a golden measuring rod to measure the city, its gates, and its wall. This provides a second, eschatological scene in which a rod and exact measurement belong together.

basis: wicked people's allotted portion in the burning lake
note: The listed wicked receive their portion in the lake burning with fire and sulfur. It brings together the commentary's two final terms, allotted share and the great fire, in one eschatological sentence.

basis: measure of faith allotted to each
note: The commentary's source gloss gives قدر the sense of setting a measure and each person's share; Paul says God has allotted each a measure of faith, a direct Christian example of individualized measure without claiming identical doctrine.

basis: God apportions a measure of faith to each
note: Each person is to think according to the measure of faith God apportioned. The verse turns the commentary's measure-and-share vocabulary into a differentiated divine gift rather than a prize won by chance.

basis: two spirits appointed for people to walk in until visitation
note: The Community Rule says God appoints two spirits in which humans walk until the time of visitation. Its measured duration and directed paths make a specific Second Temple comparison for the commentary's divine determination, guidance, and consequential choice.

basis: everything in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven
note: The Talmud's maxim reserves fear of Heaven from what is in Heaven's hands. It places 87:10's fear within a Jewish distinction between divine determination and responsible response.

basis: a heavenly mazal tells each blade of grass to grow
note: The midrash says no blade of grass lacks a heavenly mazal that strikes it and says, Grow. It develops divine guidance of created life at the creaturely level, giving a Jewish interpretive analogue to قدر then هدى.

basis: Torah as plan consulted before creation
note: The commentary reads creation as craft with planning before shaping; Genesis Rabbah compares a king consulting an architect's plan before building a palace with God consulting Torah before creating the world, supplying a Jewish interpretation of creation as planned workmanship.

basis: all foreseen, yet freedom of choice given
note: Avot holds together divine foreknowledge and granted human choice. This is a concise Jewish formulation for reading the commentary's measured determination without collapsing its final moral choosing into fatalism.

basis: dice-player disqualified from testimony
note: The Mishnah lists a player with dice among people disqualified from giving testimony. Its legal suspicion of gaming supplies a Jewish ethical counterpart to the commentary's contrast between apportioned share and maysir.

basis: lots for household portions; prohibition of gambling with others
note: The Mishnah permits household members to determine portions by lot but forbids doing so with outsiders as gambling. Its legal distinction directly illuminates the commentary's double sense of maysir as distribution of portions and condemned game.

basis: traits allotted at conception but not righteousness or wickedness
note: The Talmud imagines an angel asking what a conceived drop will become—strong or weak, wise or foolish, rich or poor—while excluding righteous or wicked. It is a precise Jewish qualification of measured human endowment that preserves the moral choice foregrounded by the commentary's final contrast.

basis: this world as a vestibule before the world to come
note: The commentary says people prefer this life although the Hereafter is better and more enduring; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for the latter, giving the preference a Jewish ethical formulation.

basis: God sees the heart rather than appearance
note: The commentary says God knows what is public and what is hidden; Samuel contrasts what humans see outwardly with YHWH's regard for the heart, specifying inward knowledge against visible appearance.

basis: humans see appearance while the Lord sees the heart
note: The Lord distinguishes human sight of outward appearance from his own sight of the heart. It is a particularly concrete counterpart to knowing the public and the concealed.

basis: an arrow beyond the boy signals David's course
note: Jonathan's cry that the arrow is beyond the boy functions as a directional signal to the hidden David. This adds a narrative use in which an arrow tells someone where danger and movement lie.

basis: arrow of the Lord's victory shot toward the east
note: Elisha orders an eastward shot and calls it the Lord's arrow of victory. It gives the fashioned arrow a prophetic target and direction, like the commentary's hearing of guidance through an arrowhead aimed ahead.

basis: plumb line set against a built wall
note: The Lord stands by a wall made with a plumb line and holds the line himself. This supplies an Israelite image of measuring straightness that turns the commentary's artisanal measuring into an evaluative act.

basis: God knows hidden things and darkness
note: God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness. This is a direct counterpart to 87:7's knowledge of what is openly spoken and what remains concealed.

basis: fixed animal portions for the priest
note: The commentary describes slaughtering a camel and sharing its pieces by game arrows, then contrasts that with a measured share from God; Deuteronomy assigns the priest the shoulder, cheeks, and stomach from an ox or sheep, a specific animal share fixed by law rather than chance.

basis: choice between life and death
note: The commentary calls 87:16–17 a choice of share between present life and the better Hereafter; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life, turning choice into an ethical decision with consequences.

basis: remembering the whole way God led in the wilderness
note: Israel is commanded to remember the whole way the Lord led it for forty years, including the testing that exposed what was in the heart. This joins remembrance, divine leading, and knowledge of the concealed interior.

basis: remember the creator before the evil days
note: Qohelet commands remembrance of the creator before the days of decline arrive. It gives the commentary's creation and reminder motifs a single temporal exhortation.

basis: every deed, including the hidden, brought to judgment
note: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden before describing the condemned person's fire; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including the hidden one, into judgment, joining hidden knowledge to accountability.

basis: hidden deeds brought into judgment
note: God will bring every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment. It adds the judicial consequence to the commentary's open-and-hidden knowledge and its ensuing fire.

basis: a time for every matter
note: Qohelet assigns a time to every matter under heaven. It closely meets the commentary's secondary claim that every thing has both a measure and an appointed term.

basis: Pur selects the date for Haman's plan
note: The commentary's arrows distribute shares by a lottery; Haman casts Pur to select a date for destroying the Jews, showing a lot used to schedule a fateful act rather than allot portions.

basis: Pur cast day by day to select a destructive date
note: Haman casts Pur, explicitly a lot, to select the day and month for his plan against the Jews. This is a sharply negative biblical lot scene beside the commentary's concern that a share sought through chance can become morally corrupt.

basis: Hebrew tzeli-esh, roasted with fire
note: The Passover flesh is to be eaten roasted with fire. Hebrew tz-l-h and Arabic s-l-y are a plausible Semitic lexical meeting for the commentary's fire verb, but the Hebrew passage concerns cooking rather than entering or straightening at a fire, so the semantic link should remain qualified.

basis: Hebrew צלה and Arabic ṣ-l-y, roasting over fire
note: The source commentary labels the Qur'anic word يَصْلَى with root ṣ-l-y and also gives a fire-working sense for straightening a stick; Exodus uses the related Hebrew roast verb for Passover meat cooked over fire, showing a cognate fire-use in its own ritual context.

basis: YHWH goes before Israel to lead them
note: The commentary says a staff is named as a guide because it precedes its bearer; Exodus pictures YHWH going before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night to lead them, making the leading-ahead image a narrative act.

basis: pillar goes before Israel to lead the way
note: The Lord goes before Israel in the pillar in order to lead them on the road. It gives a narrative form to the commentary's explanation that a leading implement receives its name from going ahead of its bearer.

basis: arrows used for divination
note: The commentary's arrows determine a game's shares, while Ezekiel's Babylonian king shakes arrows among other divinations to choose his military route; the shared arrow practice illuminates how a chance sign could direct action, though here it selects a route rather than a portion.

basis: Babylonian king shakes arrows for divination
note: At a crossroads the Babylonian king shakes arrows, consults household gods, and examines a liver to choose his route. This is the clearest biblical scene of arrow-divination beside the commentary's Qur'anic prohibition of seeking apportioned outcomes through azlam.

basis: lights appointed for signs, seasons, days, and years
note: The created lights are set in the firmament to mark signs, seasons, days, and years. This gives a creation passage in which making also establishes the measured temporal order and term developed from قدر.

basis: God Most High in Abraham's oath
note: Abraham names the creator God Most High in his oath. Hebrew Elyon and the commentary's al-A'la belong to the same highness vocabulary, while Abraham's presence answers the section's closing turn to Ibrahim.

basis: Hagar carries a skin of water into the wilderness
note: The commentary develops how a leather waterbag is measured, fitted, treated, shaken, and worn; Genesis gives a concrete narrative use of a water skin carried with a child into the wilderness, where its capacity becomes life-critical.

basis: Hagar sent out with bread and a skin of water
note: Abraham places bread and a skin of water on Hagar before sending her into the wilderness. As the necessary beginning of the later well scene, it shows the water-skin's carrying function and the vulnerability that makes its refilling significant.

basis: God opens Hagar's eyes and she fills a water-skin at the well
note: After God opens Hagar's eyes to a well, she fills the skin and gives the child water. It puts the commentary's prepared water-skin into a scene of guided provision rather than treating the vessel as a mere shared object.

basis: Hebrew halaq, smooth rather than hairy
note: Jacob calls himself a smooth man in contrast with Esau's hairiness. Hebrew h-l-q is a plausible cognate meeting for the commentary's Arabic خ ل ق in its developed smoothness sense, but the verse concerns bodily texture rather than a smoothed arrow or worn skin.

basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk and heals him
note: The commentary glosses Rab as bringing something through stages toward completion; Hosea pictures God teaching Ephraim to walk, holding him, and healing him, giving a relational image of gradual nurture.

basis: teaching Ephraim to walk, carrying him
note: God recalls teaching Ephraim to walk and taking him up in his arms. This depicts the Lord's care as gradual formation and direction, close to the commentary's ربّ as bringing something through stages to completion.

basis: a voice identifies the way to walk
note: When hearers turn right or left, a voice behind them says, This is the way; walk in it. The verse gives guidance a concrete directional utterance, like the commentary's implement aimed ahead.

basis: lot cast and land apportioned by a measuring line
note: God casts the lot for the creatures and apportions their land with a line. This unusually joins the commentary's two main operations: measured boundary-making and assigned lot.

basis: creator measures waters and heavens
note: The commentary's craft scene joins creating with sizing and straightening; Isaiah portrays the creator measuring waters, spanning heavens, and weighing mountains, giving that workmanship a cosmic scale.

basis: measured waters, heavens, dust, and mountains
note: The maker measures waters, marks off heaven, and weighs earth and mountains. Its successive hand-measurements are a close biblical counterpart to the commentary's picture of creation as skilled measuring and setting straight.

basis: crooked made straight; rough made level
note: The preparation of the Lord's way turns crooked ground straight and rough terrain level. This is the physical road-making counterpart to the commentary's سوّى as correcting crookedness before guidance.

basis: God leads the blind and levels rough places
note: The commentary joins straightening what is bent to the arrow point's guidance; Isaiah says YHWH leads the blind on an unknown road, makes darkness light, and levels rough places, combining the same two actions in a divine-guidance promise.

basis: God leads blind people and levels rough places
note: God leads those who cannot see on an unknown way and makes rough places level before them. The verse joins the two actions that the commentary keeps together: smoothing or straightening, then leading toward a way.

basis: smith works iron over coals
note: The commentary describes turning a stick over fire to straighten it and uses the same source-labeled Arabic root in 87:12's fire; Isaiah's smith works iron over coals and hammers it into shape, adding a concrete forge scene where fire serves manufacture.

basis: measured carpenter's work makes an idol
note: The commentary's opening craft scene has measuring before cutting and shaping; Isaiah describes a carpenter stretching a line, marking, planing, and using a compass to form an idol, making a pointed contrast between measured human manufacture and the Lord who creates in 87:2–3.

basis: human artisan measures and shapes an idol
note: A carpenter stretches a line, marks, planes, and compasses an image for a house. The measured craft resembles the commentary's workshop sequence, but Isaiah uses it to expose a human-made idol whereas the Qur'anic sequence predicates measured making of God.

basis: goes before and levels the way
note: God promises to go before Cyrus and level the elevated ground. Going in front, as the commentary's staff does, is paired here with making a traversable route.

basis: Hebrew שוה, making equal, and Arabic s-w-y
note: The source commentary labels سوّى with root s-w-y and explains it as straightening what is crooked; Isaiah uses the related Hebrew verb in asking whom an idol can be made equal to, adding the sense of leveling or equality in a polemic against rival images.

basis: teaching for benefit and leading in a way
note: The commentary joins the ayat's guiding verb with its reminder's benefit; Isaiah's Redeemer says he teaches what is profitable and leads in the way one should go, bringing those two actions together without implying a cognate.

basis: teaching what profits and leading the right way
note: God identifies himself as the one who teaches Israel for its profit and leads it in the way it should go. The unusual pairing directly brings 87:9's benefit together with 87:3's guidance.

basis: polished arrow and quiver
note: The commentary makes the second and third ayat sound like a shaped, straight arrow whose point leads, and separately notes a bag for arrows; Isaiah's servant is made as a polished arrow and hidden in YHWH's quiver, adding a scriptural image of divine preparation and readiness.

basis: servant made a polished arrow and hidden in a quiver
note: God makes the servant a polished arrow and conceals him in a quiver. This directly meets the commentary's smoothed arrow shaft and arrow-container, while making the fashioned projectile a figure of a divinely directed mission.

basis: God creates the smith who blows the coal fire and makes a weapon
note: The creator is said to make the smith, his coal fire, and the weapon fitted for its task. It makes the commentary's fire, straightening craft, and aimed implement part of a single divine-artisan scene.

basis: Hebrew h-l-q: smooth stones, portion, and lot
note: Isaiah plays on smooth valley stones, a person's portion, and lot in one idolatry verse. Hebrew h-l-q is a concrete Semitic cognate meeting for the commentary's Arabic خ ل ق cluster, which likewise develops smoothing and the apportioned خلاق; the cultic setting keeps the comparison specific.

basis: potter, clay, and the work of divine hands
note: Israel calls God its potter and itself the work of God's hands. It offers another concrete artisan image for the commentary's claim that creation verbs sound like stages in a maker's work.

basis: unquenched fire and an undying worm for rebels
note: The rebels' worm does not die and their fire is not quenched. It is a close Hebrew Bible counterpart to the surah's fire immediately followed by neither dying nor living.

basis: potter remakes a spoiled vessel
note: The commentary's measure-and-shape sequence evokes preparing an object toward its finished form; Jeremiah watches a potter reshape a spoiled clay vessel as seemed good to him, a concrete craft scene that makes re-forming part of the maker's work.

basis: Israel as clay in the potter's hand
note: The commentary's creation verbs are framed as a maker forming and ordering material; Jeremiah explicitly applies the potter-and-clay scene to YHWH and Israel, turning craft into a claim about the maker's authority over a people.

basis: fixed days and set bounds
note: The commentary gives قدر the secondary sense of a thing's amount and term; Job says a person's days are fixed, months numbered, and limit set, making the finite term a specific instance of divinely measured life.

basis: a boundary inscribed on the waters at light's limit
note: God draws a boundary on the face of the waters at the limit between light and darkness. The image is a precise act of measured delimitation within creation, extending the commentary's maker scene beyond tools and objects.

basis: wind weighed and waters measured
note: The commentary reads creation through measuring before shaping; Job says God assigned weight to wind and measure to waters, making measure itself part of divine ordering.

basis: wind weighed; waters measured
note: God gives the wind a weight and apportions waters by measure. The verse makes cosmic making an act of exact weighting and measurement, matching the commentary's maker sequence rather than a generic creation claim.

basis: new wineskins ready to burst
note: Elihu compares pent-up speech to wine without a vent, like new wineskins ready to burst. This gives the leather vessel a dynamic of internal pressure, a distinct material counterpart to the commentary's shaken and worked skin.

basis: earth measured with a line
note: The commentary links creation to an artisan's measured preparation; Job's creation challenge asks who fixed earth's measurements and stretched a line upon it, giving the image of measurement a concrete construction tool.

basis: Creator fixes earth's measurements and stretches a line
note: Job's creator asks who set the earth's measures and stretched the measuring line over it. It supplies the same concrete move from creating to proportioning that the commentary hears in خلق followed by قدّر.

basis: lots identify the cause of a calamity
note: The commentary describes arrows drawing shares in a game; the sailors cast lots to discover whose account brought the storm, and the lot falls on Jonah, a distinct use of chance to identify responsibility rather than divide goods.

basis: sailors cast lots to identify the cause of disaster
note: The sailors cast lots to discover on whose account the storm has come. This is a specific narrative analogue to seeking a hidden judgment through a lot, the sort of divinatory use that makes the Qur'anic ban on arrow-lots intelligible.

basis: lot divides an inheritance
note: The commentary says the game arrows distribute portions and that this chance share is forbidden; Joshua has Israel receive its territorial inheritance by lot before YHWH, a concrete sacred allotment with a different function.

basis: surveyed land in seven divisions followed by lots
note: Joshua orders a written division of the land into seven parts and then casts lots before the Lord. It combines prior measurement and description with the distribution of shares by lot, just as the commentary moves from measure to apportioned portions.

basis: wineskins worn out through use
note: The Gibeonites display wineskins that were new when filled but are now worn out. This is a concrete biblical analogue to the commentary's account of a leather vessel becoming smooth and spent through use.

basis: worn, torn, and patched wineskins
note: The commentary's waterbag is measured, fitted with side pieces, treated, and eventually worn smooth; Joshua's travelers carry old wineskins that are worn, torn, and patched, a concrete scriptural witness to the used leather vessel.

basis: lots assign the goats' ritual roles
note: The commentary rejects the meysir arrows used to assign shares; Leviticus uses lots to distinguish the goat for YHWH from the one for Azazel, showing a ritual allocation rather than gambling.

basis: Aaron's two ritual lots for the goats
note: Aaron casts lots to distinguish the goat for the Lord from the goat for Azazel. The regulated cultic lot is a useful counterpoint to the commentary's prohibited lot-arrows, because the difference in ritual setting is the point.

basis: those who fear God and a book of remembrance
note: Those who fear the Lord are heard, and a book of remembrance is written before him. The verse specifically links fear with remembrance, the sequence named in 87:9-10.

basis: fire as refining and purification
note: The commentary links the staff straightened over fire to the same fire entered by the condemned in 87:12; Malachi's refiner-fire purifies the Levites, giving fire a restorative craft function rather than a punitive end.

basis: refiner's fire purifying metal
note: The Lord sits as a refiner and purifier of silver to cleanse the Levites. It gives fire an artisan's transformative function, close to the commentary's fire used to straighten a staff, while retaining its own priestly context.

basis: inheritance divided by lot among named tribes
note: Israel's land inheritance is divided by lot according to ancestral names. The text gives a non-gambling form of the commentary's measured share: a durable allotted possession.

basis: a leader who goes out before and brings the people in
note: Moses asks for a leader who will go out before the congregation, bring them out and in, so they will not be sheep without a shepherd. It makes the before-going action a responsible form of guidance in the Moses context named at the end of the surah.

basis: lot cast, decision from YHWH
note: The commentary treats the game arrows as assigning shares by chance and contrasts them with the share set by God; Proverbs says a lot is cast but its decision belongs to YHWH, so the lot is not an independent force.

basis: lot cast, but its decision from the Lord
note: Proverbs says a lot is cast into the lap while every judgment of it comes from the Lord. Against the commentary's ban on divinatory arrows, it supplies a contrasting Israelite maxim that assigns a cast lot's outcome to divine decision.

basis: human planning and divine direction
note: The commentary's artisan first thinks through how to prepare and straighten an object, then turns to guidance; Proverbs says a person plans a way but YHWH establishes the steps, a close sequence of planning followed by direction.

basis: human planning and the Lord establishing steps
note: A person's heart plans a way, but the Lord establishes the steps. This compresses the commentary's pondering of how to prepare a matter and the subsequent divine directing of its course.

basis: crooked ways made straight
note: The commentary's arrow-making scene joins straightening what is bent to directing its point; Proverbs says YHWH makes a person's paths straight, bringing straightness and guidance together in a path image.

basis: teaching a way of wisdom and leading in upright tracks
note: The parental teacher says, I have taught you the way of wisdom and led you in upright tracks. Its joined teaching, leading, and straight path provide a sapiential counterpart to measured preparation followed by guidance.

basis: avoid, turn away from, and pass beyond the wicked path
note: The father repeatedly commands avoidance of the wicked path: do not enter it, turn away, and pass on. Its verbs give a concrete path-image for the commentary's yatajannabuha, even though the object there is the reminder.

basis: the sea's limit and earth's foundations marked out
note: Wisdom recalls God assigning the sea a limit so its waters do not transgress and marking the earth's foundations. It specifies measurement as a boundary that guides created elements in their proper course.

basis: reproof helps the wise but provokes the scoffer
note: Reproof is hated by a scoffer but loved by the wise. It gives a close sapiential analogue to the commentary's conditional reminder: the same admonition benefits a receptive person and is rejected by another.

basis: a wineskin in smoke and remembrance
note: The commentary separately describes a waterbag becoming smooth with use and a reminder that may benefit; the psalmist likens himself to a wineskin in smoke yet says he has not forgotten God's statutes, joining a worn vessel image to remembering, though the psalm's image is distress rather than ordinary use.

basis: wineskin in smoke that does not forget statutes
note: The speaker has become like a wineskin in smoke but does not forget God's statutes. It tightly joins the commentary's weathered leather vessel with its later concern for a remembrance that remains effective.

basis: sons compared to arrows in a warrior's hand
note: The commentary develops a shaped arrow and a quiver-like container; the psalm compares sons of youth to arrows in a warrior's hand, adding a family image in which the prepared arrow represents offspring ready for action.

basis: unformed days recorded beforehand
note: The commentary says every thing has an amount and term; the psalmist says his unformed substance and all his days were seen and written before they arrived, joining formation to a measured lifespan.

basis: God knows a word before it is spoken
note: The commentary names both what is aloud and what is hidden as known to God; the psalmist says God knows his word before it reaches his tongue, extending the claim to speech not yet made public.

basis: stars counted and named
note: The commentary connects creation with measuring and assigning each thing its share; the psalm says God counts the stars and calls them by name, a concrete image of creation known and ordered individually.

basis: the Lord as portion, cup, and lot
note: The commentary distinguishes the game's allotted share from the share given by the measure-setter; the psalmist calls YHWH his portion, cup, and lot, recasting allotment as trust in God rather than a game.

basis: measured boundary lines and secure inheritance
note: The commentary says an arrow-game share is measured out and contrasts it with the enduring Hereafter; the psalmist's boundary lines fall in pleasant places and his inheritance is secure, a fixed inheritance rather than a chance stake.

basis: God as the speaker's portion and holder of his lot
note: The psalm calls the Lord the speaker's portion and cup and says that God holds his lot. It provides a theological alternative to a self-sought gambling share: the decisive portion is received from God.

basis: garments divided and clothing allotted by lot
note: The commentary's game divides a slaughtered camel into portions chosen by arrows; the psalm describes people dividing garments and casting lots for clothing, a specific allocation scene without the game's animal shares.

basis: restored and led on right paths
note: The commentary links the Lord's completing care with guidance and describes a staff that goes ahead of its bearer; the psalm's shepherd restores the speaker and leads him on right paths, combining care and direction.

basis: Hebrew עליון and Arabic al-aʿlā, the Most High
note: The commentary's ayah calls God al-Aʿlā and notes that the same Arabic root names the highest game arrow; the psalm calls YHWH Most High over all the earth, so a related Semitic height term belongs to divine supremacy here, not a gaming share.

basis: refusal to listen, turned shoulder, and stopped ears
note: The ancestors refuse to pay attention, turn a stubborn shoulder, and make their ears too heavy to hear prophetic instruction. This is a close narrative profile of keeping away from a reminder.

basis: measure, number, and weight
note: The commentary links خلق and قدر as making and setting a measure; Wisdom says God ordered all things by measure, number, and weight, an unusually exact Jewish formulation of creation as measured order.

basis: measure, number, and weight
note: Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. This gives an explicit Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that created things have a determined measure.
